COUNTY RESTAURANT CLEANING AND SANITATION STANDARDS  
2026 Regulatory Compliance Handbook  
Issued by: County Environmental Health & Sanitation Division  

INTRODUCTION  
Restaurants, food vendors, and commercial kitchens must adhere to strict cleaning and sanitation standards to prevent the spread of foodborne illness. This document forms the official county guidelines for cleaning frequency, chemical usage, equipment maintenance, water safety, waste disposal, and emergency response. Failure to follow these standards may result in citations, fines, or temporary closure of the establishment.

This handbook must be reviewed quarterly by the Person-In-Charge (PIC), and all employees must receive training on relevant sections.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 1 — DAILY CLEANING REQUIREMENTS
------------------------------------------------------------

1.1 Prep Areas  
All preparation surfaces must be cleaned and sanitized after each task and at least every four hours during continuous use. Cutting boards must be washed using hot, soapy water followed by sanitizing using an approved solution. Wet boards must be air-dried before reuse.

1.2 Cooking Equipment  
Cooking equipment—including grills, fryers, flat-tops, ovens, sandwich presses, and steamers—must be wiped at the end of each shift. Grease buildup must be completely removed from grill edges, fryer walls, and underneath stovetops. Grease accumulation is a major contributor to pest attraction and fire hazards.

1.3 Refrigerators and Freezers  
Spills or leaks must be cleaned immediately. Shelves must be wiped daily using food-safe detergent. Refrigerator door gaskets must be inspected for mold, tears, and residue accumulation. Freezer condensation must be monitored to prevent frost buildup impacting door closure.

1.4 Sinks  
Handwashing sinks must remain unobstructed. Prep sinks must be cleaned after each use. Three-compartment dishwashing sinks must be washed and sanitized at least once daily, including faucet handles.

1.5 Floors  
Kitchen floors must be swept and mopped daily. Mop water must be changed as soon as visibly dirty or after cleaning waste areas. Mop sink drainage must be free of standing water.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 2 — WEEKLY CLEANING REQUIREMENTS
------------------------------------------------------------

2.1 Exhaust Hood and Filters  
Kitchen exhaust hoods accumulate grease from steam and smoke. Filters must be removed weekly and washed. Persistent residue requires degreaser and hot water soak.

2.2 Storage Shelves  
Dry storage shelves must be sanitized weekly. Unlabeled items must be discarded. Shelves must be organized to prevent food from being stacked in ways that restrict airflow.

2.3 Drains  
All floor drains must be scrubbed with brushes weekly. Drain covers must be removed to clean internal components.

2.4 Trash Room  
Indoor trash storage areas must be deep cleaned weekly. Floors must be sanitized and residues from food scraps removed.

2.5 Beverage Machines  
Coffee brewers, soda machines, and water dispensers must be flushed weekly. Drip trays must be cleaned and sanitized.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 3 — MONTHLY CLEANING REQUIREMENTS
------------------------------------------------------------

3.1 Behind Large Appliances  
Areas behind ovens, fryers, grills, and refrigerators must be cleaned monthly. Dust and grease buildup attracts pests and impedes airflow.

3.2 Ceiling Vents and Panels  
Ceiling vents must be vacuumed monthly. If grease buildup is visible, vents must be removed and washed thoroughly.

3.3 Storage Reassessment  
All dry goods must be rotated monthly.

Expired herbs, spices, and packaged foods must be discarded.

3.4 Ice Machine  
Ice tray compartments must be deep-cleaned monthly. Mold residue is a common issue in neglected machines.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 4 — FOOD TEMPERATURE AND HOLDING REQUIREMENTS
------------------------------------------------------------

4.1 Cold Holding  
All refrigerated foods must be kept at 41°F or below. Cut leafy greens, tomatoes, melons, and dairy-based sauces are considered highly perishable and must remain below this threshold. Cold holding temperatures must be verified twice per shift.

4.2 Hot Holding  
Foods kept hot must remain at 135°F or above. Steam tables must be monitored frequently. Warmers must not be overloaded to ensure even heat distribution.

4.3 Cooling Requirements  
The following cooling timeline is mandatory:
- 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours  
- 70°F to 41°F within 4 hours  
Food exceeding these thresholds must be discarded. Cooling logs must be maintained.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 5 — CHEMICAL SAFETY AND STORAGE
------------------------------------------------------------

5.1 Approved Chemicals  
Approved sanitizers include quaternary ammonium compounds, chlorine-based cleaners, and iodine solutions. Detergents must be food-safe for kitchen equipment. Bleach must be diluted appropriately.

5.2 Chemical Placement  
Chemicals must never be stored above food items or equipment. Spray bottles must have clearly marked labels.

Unlabeled chemicals must be discarded immediately. Chemical shelving must be cleaned weekly.

5.3 Sanitizer Strength Testing  
Sanitizer buckets must be tested at least twice daily using appropriate test strips. Strength requirements:
- Quat: 200–400 ppm  
- Chlorine: 50–100 ppm  

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 6 — WATER SAFETY AND PLUMBING
------------------------------------------------------------

6.1 Potable Water Requirements  
Restaurants must have access to potable water at all times. If water service is interrupted, restaurant operations must cease until restored.

6.2 Hot Water Availability  
Hot water temperature for dishwashing must reach at least 120°F. If temperatures cannot be reached, dishwashing sinks cannot be used until water is restored.

6.3 Drainage  
Drain blockages must be resolved immediately. Standing water in floor drains is considered a critical violation due to contamination risk.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 7 — WASTE DISPOSAL REQUIREMENTS
------------------------------------------------------------

7.1 Indoor Waste  
Waste bins must:
- Remain covered  
- Be emptied frequently  
- Be cleaned and sanitized daily  

Food scraps must never accumulate around bin edges. Wet waste bags must be double‑bagged.

7.2 Outdoor Waste  
All dumpsters must remain closed. Grease trap containers must be inspected daily for overflow. Waste areas must remain free of debris to prevent pest attraction.

7.3 Hazardous Waste  
Oil and grease disposal must follow county environmental guidelines. Grease containers must be placed on stable surfaces away from foot traffic.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 8 — PEST CONTROL REGULATIONS
------------------------------------------------------------

8.1 Contractor Requirements  
Restaurants must use licensed pest control contractors. Visits must occur monthly or quarterly depending on facility size. Reports must be retained for one year.

8.2 Internal Monitoring  
Employees must document:
- Live insect sightings  
- Droppings  
- Gnaw marks  
- Grease trails  
- Damaged packaging  
- Nesting materials  

8.3 Mitigation  
If pest activity is observed, immediate actions include:
- Deep cleaning affected areas  
- Removing contaminated food  
- Repairing wall or floor cracks  
- Scheduling contractor visit within 48 hours  

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 9 — EMERGENCY CONDITIONS REQUIRING TEMPORARY CLOSURE
------------------------------------------------------------

The following situations require **immediate closure** of a restaurant:

9.1 Sewage Backup  
Any sewage overflow or backup inside the facility requires immediate closure until full sanitization and reinspection.

9.2 Power Outage  
If food temperatures cannot be maintained due to power loss, closure is required. Foods that exceed safe temperature limits must be discarded.

9.3 Water Service Interruption  
If potable water is unavailable, the facility must close.

Bottled water may only be used for limited functions with prior health department approval.

9.4 Rodent Infestation  
Presence of live rodents constitutes a critical violation. Signs of rodents include droppings, nesting material, grease marks, and gnawing. Closure remains until pest control clears the facility.

9.5 Structural Hazard  
Ceiling collapse risk, unstable shelving, or unsafe flooring conditions require immediate closure until repairs are verified by inspectors.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 10 — INSPECTOR CHECKLIST FOR ROUTINE VISITS
------------------------------------------------------------

Inspectors must review:
- Temperature logs  
- Sanitizer strength measurements  
- Equipment cleanliness  
- Pest control logs  
- Employee hygiene practices  
- Waste disposal condition  
- Drainage systems  
- Compliance with cooling procedures  
- Chemical storage
- Date labels and FIFO rotation  
- Gasket condition  
- Ice machine cleanliness  
- Vent condition  

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 11 — MANAGEMENT RESPONSIBILITIES
------------------------------------------------------------

The Person-In-Charge (PIC) must:
- Maintain all logs  
- Conduct employee training  
- Document violations and corrective actions  
- Ensure pest control scheduling  
- Oversee cleaning tasks  
- Respond to inspector warnings promptly  
- Report structural issues immediately  
- Verify throat clearance of grease traps  
- Check handwashing supply stock  

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 12 — STAFF TRAINING REQUIREMENTS
------------------------------------------------------------

Training must address:
- Hygiene practices  
- Cleaning schedules  
- Cross-contamination risks  
- Food temperature rules  
- Chemical handling  
- Emergency response  
- Pest control basics  

Training must be documented with employee signatures and dates.

------------------------------------------------------------
CONCLUSION  
These cleaning and sanitation standards form the backbone of safe restaurant operations. All staff must follow these guidelines daily, weekly, and monthly. Failure to comply may result in citations, fines, or temporary facility closure.
END OF DOCUMENT

HYGIENE TRAINING MANUAL FOR FOOD SERVICE EMPLOYEES  
County Department of Environmental Health  
2026 Standardized Employee Training Module  

OVERVIEW  
This hygiene manual provides detailed guidelines for all employees who handle food in commercial establishments. These guidelines are intended to reduce contamination risks, promote safe food handling, and ensure consistent compliance with county food safety laws. All employees must complete this training before performing any food preparation tasks.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 1 — INTRODUCTION TO FOOD SAFETY
------------------------------------------------------------

1.1 What is Food Safety?  
Food safety refers to the handling, preparation, and storage practices that prevent foodborne illnesses. Safe food handling protects customers, the restaurant, and the community.

1.2 Employee Responsibilities  
Employees must:
- Follow personal hygiene requirements  
- Maintain clean workstations  
- Report contamination events  
- Follow glove and handwashing rules  
- Prevent cross-contamination  

1.3 Person-In-Charge (PIC) Overview  
The Person-In-Charge is responsible for ensuring training, verifying compliance, documenting corrective actions, and responding to inspector feedback.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 2 — HANDWASHING AND GLOVE REQUIREMENTS
------------------------------------------------------------

2.1 Handwashing Basics  
Proper handwashing is a critical component of hygiene:
- Use warm water and soap  
- Scrub hands for at least 20 seconds  
- Rinse thoroughly  
- Dry with paper towels  
Handwashing must occur before beginning food prep and after contamination.

2.2 When Handwashing is Required  
Employees must wash hands:
- After using the restroom  
- After touching hair, face, clothing, phones  
- After handling raw meat, poultry, or eggs  
- After touching trash or cleaning supplies  
- Before switching between tasks  
- Before applying gloves  

2.3 Glove Rules  
Gloves are required when handling ready-to-eat foods.  
Gloves must be changed:
- After touching raw foods  
- After touching non-food items  
- When torn or damaged  
- At least every 4 hours during continuous use  

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 3 — PERSONAL CLEANLINESS
------------------------------------------------------------

3.1 Clothing  
Employees must wear clean uniforms or aprons. Clothing that becomes soiled must be replaced immediately.

3.2 Hair Restraints  
Hair restraints must be worn at all times. Hair nets, hats, or tied-back coverings are acceptable. Loose hair poses a contamination risk.

3.3 Jewelry  
Jewelry can harbor bacteria:
- No rings except plain bands  
- No bracelets  
- No dangling items that may contact food  

3.4 Illness Policies  
Employees must report symptoms of diarrhea, vomiting, fever, or jaundice. The PIC must exclude ill employees from food handling duties.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 4 — CLEAN WORK ENVIRONMENT
------------------------------------------------------------

4.1 Maintaining Prep Areas  
Prep tables must remain clean and sanitized. Wiping cloths must be stored in sanitizer buckets with appropriate concentration levels. All utensils must be sanitized after each use.

4.2 Cutting Boards and Equipment  
Cutting boards must be sanitized after each use. Deep grooves in boards require replacement. Equipment such as mixers, blenders, slicers, and processors must be cleaned thoroughly after each task.

4.3 Storage Practices  
Food must be stored at least 6 inches above the floor to prevent contamination. Containers must be clearly labeled and sealed securely. Ready-to-eat foods must always be kept above raw ingredients.

4.4 Temperature Awareness  
Employees must understand safe temperature ranges:
- Cold foods: 41°F or below  
- Hot foods: 135°F or above  
- Cooling from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F within 4 hours  

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 5 — PREVENTING CROSS-CONTAMINATION
------------------------------------------------------------

5.1 Raw vs Cooked Foods  
Raw chicken, beef, seafood, and eggs must be handled separately from ready-to-eat foods. Separate utensils, cutting boards, and containers must be used.

5.2 Handling Utensils  
Utensils must be washed, rinsed, and sanitized at regular intervals. Knives must not be placed in sinks or on cutting boards after use without washing.

5.3 Chemical Storage  
Chemicals must never be stored near food. Cleaning sprays and sanitizers must be labeled and stored away from prep areas.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 6 — FOOD PROTECTION PRACTICES
------------------------------------------------------------

6.1 Protecting Ready-to-Eat Foods  
Ready-to-eat foods must remain covered when not actively prepared. Sneeze guards must be used for buffets. Employees must avoid bare-hand contact.

6.2 Cooling and Reheating  
Cooling must follow county standards. Food reheated for hot-holding must reach at least 165°F. Leftovers must be cooled quickly using shallow pans or ice baths.

6.3 Preventing Spoilage  
Signs of spoilage include:
- Off-odors  
- Discoloration  
- Mold  
- Dryness or cracking in sweets  
Employees must report food spoilage immediately.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 7 — HYGIENE DURING BUSY PERIODS
------------------------------------------------------------

Busy periods increase the risk of contamination. Employees must:
- Switch gloves frequently  
- Follow time-based cleaning schedules  
- Avoid rushing food prep  
- Keep spills cleaned immediately  

Employees must never skip handwashing during busy hours.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 8 — WASTE AND DISPOSAL PRACTICES
------------------------------------------------------------

8.1 Indoor Waste  
Waste bins must remain closed at all times. Food scraps must never accumulate around bin edges.

Bins must be emptied frequently.

8.2 Outdoor Waste  
Outdoor waste bins and dumpsters must be sealed.

Grease traps must be checked for overflow and cleaned regularly.

8.3 Mop Sink and Drain Areas  
Drain areas must remain free of standing water. Mop sinks must be cleaned daily.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 9 — TRAINING VERIFICATION AND DOCUMENTATION
------------------------------------------------------------

9.1 Training Records  
Training logs must include employee signatures, dates, and completed modules. Managers must maintain training records for at least 12 months.

9.2 Corrective Actions  
Managers must document corrective actions when employees fail to follow hygiene rules. Employees must re-attend training sessions if repeated violations occur.

9.3 Ongoing Education  
Employees must receive refresher training annually. Updates to food safety laws must be communicated promptly.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 10 — SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------

Employee hygiene is essential to safe food operations. Restaurants must ensure that staff maintain proper handwashing, glove usage, attire, work area cleanliness, temperature awareness, and waste management.

Consistent hygiene protects customers and supports compliance with county regulations.

END OF DOCUMENT

PEST CONTROL REQUIREMENTS FOR FOOD SERVICE ESTABLISHMENTS  
County Environmental Health Department  
2026 Food Safety Compliance Manual

INTRODUCTION  
Pest activity in food facilities poses significant risks to public health, contaminates food supplies, damages structural components, and jeopardizes regulatory compliance. Restaurants must implement comprehensive pest‑control protocols designed to prevent infestation, monitor activity, and respond rapidly to any signs of pests. This document outlines the official county standards for pest prevention, identification, mitigation, and contractor oversight.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 1 — PREVENTIVE STRUCTURAL MEASURES
------------------------------------------------------------

1.1 Building Integrity  
All food establishments must maintain structural integrity to prevent pest entry:
- Door sweeps must be tight-fitting with no gaps.
- Windows must have intact screens.
- Cracks in walls, ceilings, and flooring must be sealed using approved sealants.
- Vents must include mesh coverings with openings no greater than 1/4 inch.

1.2 Exterior Maintenance  
The exterior perimeter of the restaurant must be kept clean:
- Landscaping must not touch the building structure.
- Standing water must be eliminated.
- Dumpsters must be placed at least 10 feet away from exterior walls.
- Grease spills must be removed immediately, including around outdoor containers.

1.3 Delivery and Receiving Doors  
Receiving doors must remain closed when not in use. Food deliveries must be inspected for signs of contamination such as:
- Punctured packaging
- Rodent gnaw marks
- Insect presence inside containers
- Damp or moldy boxes

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 2 — COMMON PESTS FOUND IN RESTAURANTS
------------------------------------------------------------

2.1 Rodents  
Rodents are among the most dangerous pests in food service facilities. Signs include:
- Droppings resembling small black pellets
- Grease marks along walls
- Gnawed packaging
- Shredded materials indicating nesting
- Scratching sounds near storage areas

Rodents contaminate food preparation surfaces and carry pathogens. Immediate action is required upon detection.

2.2 Cockroaches  
Cockroaches thrive in moist environments, particularly near drains.

Signs include:
- Shed skins
- Egg casings (oothecae)
- Musty odor
- Sightings of live insects during the day (indicates severe infestation)

Cockroaches can contaminate food-contact surfaces and trigger allergenic reactions.

2.3 Ants  
Ant infestations are commonly linked to poor waste management. Signs include:
- Lines of ants near soda machines, spills, or sugary residues
- Presence near storage shelves
- Small piles of sawdust-like debris (possible nesting material)

2.4 Flies  
Fruit flies and drain flies are indicators of sanitation issues:
- Fruit flies hover near waste bins and sugary spills.
- Drain flies emerge from slow-moving or dirty drains.

2.5 Beetles  
Beetles often target grain-based foods. They may appear near flour sacks or dry storage areas.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 3 — INTERNAL PREVENTION PRACTICES
------------------------------------------------------------

3.1 Food Storage Practices  
- Store food at least 6 inches off the floor.
- Keep flour, sugar, rice, and grain products in sealed containers.
- Rotate food items following FIFO (First In, First Out).
- Inspect bulk ingredients weekly for signs of pests.

3.2 Waste Control  
Improper waste management is a primary cause of pest activity:
- Indoor waste bins must be sealed and emptied regularly.
- Outdoor bins must remain closed.
- Spills near waste bins must be cleaned immediately.
- Mop rooms must remain free of standing water.

3.3 Cleaning Protocols  
Cleanliness strongly correlates with pest presence:
- Prep surfaces must be sanitized frequently.
- Floors must be swept and mopped daily.
- Drains must be scrubbed weekly or after signs of pest activity.
- Grease traps must be monitored weekly.

3.4 Equipment Storage  
Store cleaning equipment properly:
- Mops must be hung to dry.
- Buckets must be emptied and sanitized.
- Brooms must be stored away from food-storage areas.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 4 — IDENTIFICATION AND MONITORING PROTOCOLS
------------------------------------------------------------

4.1 Daily Monitoring  
Daily monitoring must document:
- Live pest sightings
- Droppings
- Damaged packaging
- Unusual odors
- Grease trails
- Activity around drains and waste bins

4.2 Weekly Monitoring  
Weekly monitoring must include:
- Inspection of dry storage shelves
- Inspection of soda and beverage machines
- Inspection of floor drains
- Review of pest-control logs

4.3 Monitoring Tools  
Approved tools include:
- Glue traps
- UV light traps
- Rodent bait stations (only by licensed contractors)
- Monitoring boards placed near drains and waste bins

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 5 — CORRECTIVE ACTION AND RESPONSE PROTOCOL
------------------------------------------------------------

5.1 Immediate Response  
Upon detecting pest activity, the employee must:
- Notify the Person-In-Charge (PIC)
- Dispose of contaminated food
- Clean the affected area thoroughly
- Document findings in the pest-control log

5.2 Contractor Response  
Licensed pest-control contractors must be contacted when:
- Evidence of rodents is detected
- Cockroaches are found in food prep areas
- Flies emerge in large numbers
- Beetles contaminate dry goods

Contractor visits must occur within 48 hours of major findings.

5.3 Deep Cleaning Requirements  
For major pest incidents:
- All prep surfaces must be sanitized.
- All food-contact equipment must be washed.
- Drains must be scrubbed thoroughly.

- Storage shelves must be reorganized.
- Waste bins must be sanitized.
- Floors must be deep-cleaned using degreaser.

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 6 — PREVENTION THROUGH EMPLOYEE PRACTICES
------------------------------------------------------------

6.1 Employee Training  
Employees must be trained to recognize:
- Rodent droppings
- Egg casings
- Nesting materials
- Gnawed packaging
- Beetle contamination

6.2 Hygiene Practices  
- Employees must wash hands before touching clean equipment.
- Gloves must be changed frequently.
- Employees must avoid leaving spills unattended.
- Sweat, hair, or clothing contamination must be avoided.

6.3 Reporting  
Employees must report:
- Unusual sounds behind walls
- Gaps in doors or windows
- Areas with persistent moisture
- Fruit fly clusters

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 7 — CRITICAL VIOLATIONS AND TEMPORARY CLOSURE
------------------------------------------------------------

A restaurant must be **temporarily closed** if any of the following occur:
- Live rodent sightings inside the food prep area
- Heavy cockroach infestation
- Pest contamination of ready-to-eat foods
- Sewage backup that attracts pests
- Significant grease overflow near dumpsters
- Structural gaps allowing pest entry
- Repeated pest sightings over multiple days without corrective action

Closure remains in effect until:
- Contractor assessment is complete
- Violations are corrected
- Inspector verifies compliance

------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 8 — DOCUMENTATION AND LOG REQUIREMENTS
------------------------------------------------------------

Log entries must include:
- Date
- Time
- Type of pest observed
- Location
- Corrective action taken
- Staff initials

Logs must be retained for at least 12 months and made available during inspections.

------------------------------------------------------------
CONCLUSION  
Pest prevention is an essential component of food safety. Restaurants that maintain strong sanitation practices, waste control, and monitoring protocols significantly reduce the risk of infestation. These standards must be followed daily to ensure compliance and protect public health.
END OF DOCUMENT

RESTAURANT FOOD SAFETY GUIDELINES – COUNTY PUBLIC HEALTH DEPARTMENT
Edition: 2026 Compliance Handbook
Applicable To: All food service establishments including restaurants, cafes, bakeries, food trucks, school cafeterias, and temporary food vendors.

INTRODUCTION
Food safety is a central pillar of public health. These guidelines outline the standards that must be followed by all commercial food establishments to prevent contamination, maintain hygiene, and ensure the well-being of customers. All restaurant managers and food handlers must familiarize themselves with these regulations and ensure compliance at all times.

SECTION 1 — PERSONAL HYGIENE REQUIREMENTS
1.1 Handwashing Protocol  
- Hands must be washed:
  * Before beginning food preparation  
  * After handling raw meat, poultry, seafood, or eggs  
  * After using the restroom  
  * After touching the face, hair, phone, or personal items  
  * After handling trash, cleaning supplies, or dirty dishes  
- Handwashing must be performed using warm water and soap for at least 20 seconds.  
- Hand sanitizer is not a substitute for handwashing. It may be used only after handwashing.

1.2 Employee Clothing and Protective Gear  
- All employees must wear clean clothing and aprons.  
- Hair restraints are required at all times.  
- Jewelry on hands and wrists should be minimized to avoid contamination.  
- Gloves must be worn when handling ready-to-eat foods.

1.3 Illness and Work Restrictions  
- Employees exhibiting symptoms of vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or contagious illnesses must be excluded from food handling tasks.  
- The Person-In-Charge (PIC) must maintain a written log of illness exclusions.

SECTION 2 — FOOD STORAGE REQUIREMENTS
2.1 Temperature Control  
- Cold foods must be held at 41°F or below.  
- Hot foods must be held at 135°F or above.  
- Frozen foods must remain frozen until ready for thawing.  
- Temperature logs must be maintained and verified twice per shift.

2.2 Cross-Contamination Prevention  
- Raw foods must be stored below ready-to-eat foods.  
- Cutting boards must be color-coded or labeled for specific uses.  
- Containers must be sealed and clearly labeled.  
- Chemicals must never be stored above or near food items.

2.3 Dry Storage  
- All ingredients must be stored at least 6 inches above the floor.  
- Shelves should be cleaned monthly or more frequently as needed.  
- Food items must be stored in pest-resistant containers.

SECTION 3 — THAWING AND COOLING PROCEDURES
3.1 Approved Methods for Thawing  
- Under refrigeration at 41°F or below  
- Under cold running water not exceeding 70°F  
- In microwave followed by immediate cooking  
- As part of the cooking process

3.2 Cooling Requirements  
Foods must be cooled from:
- 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours  
- 70°F to 41°F within 4 additional hours  
Total cooling time may not exceed 6 hours.

Shallow pans, ice baths, and blast chillers should be used to accelerate safe cooling.

SECTION 4 — SANITATION AND CLEANING STANDARDS
4.1 Cleaning Schedule  
Restaurants must maintain a written cleaning schedule. The following items require daily cleaning:
- Prep surfaces  
- Cutting boards  
- Sinks  
- Grill surfaces  
- Microwave interiors  
- Floor drains  
- Food-contact utensils

Weekly cleaning tasks include:
- Exhaust hoods  
- Refrigeration gaskets  
- Storage shelves  
- Beverage dispenser drip trays  
- Trash room and bin surfaces

Monthly cleaning tasks include:
- Ceiling vents  
- Behind large appliances (grill, fryers, ovens)  
- Drain traps  
- Ice machine interior surfaces

4.2 Approved Sanitizers  
- Quaternary ammonia (Quat) at 200–400 ppm  
- Chlorine bleach at 50–100 ppm  
- Hot water sanitization at 171°F or higher

Test strips must be used to verify sanitizer strength.

SECTION 5 — EQUIPMENT MAINTENANCE
5.1 Food Thermometers  
- Must be calibrated weekly  
- Must be cleaned and sanitized before and after each use  
- Logs must document calibration

5.2 Refrigeration Units  
- Temperature monitoring twice per shift  
- Gaskets inspected bi-weekly  
- Units must be free from excessive frost  

5.3 Deep Fryers  
- Oil must be replaced based on clarity and particulate levels  
- Fryers must be cleaned according to manufacturer guidelines

SECTION 6 — WASTE AND GARBAGE CONTROL
6.1 Indoor Waste  
- Lids must remain closed at all times  
- Trash should be removed every 4 hours or as needed  
- Waste bins must be cleaned daily

6.2 Outdoor Waste  
- Dumpsters must remain sealed  
- Grease containers must be inspected daily for leaks  
- Waste areas must be free of debris to prevent pest attraction

6.3 Grease Trap Maintenance  
- Traps should be emptied based on usage volume  
- Overflow can attract pests and violate sanitation laws

SECTION 7 — PEST CONTROL STANDARDS
7.1 Preventive Measures  
- All openings such as doors and windows must have tight seals  
- Cracks in walls or floors must be repaired promptly  
- Food must never be stored directly on the floor

7.2 Signs of Pest Activity  
- Droppings  
- Gnaw marks  
- Live insects  
- Grease trails  
- Damaged packaging  
- Nesting materials  

7.3 Contractor Requirements  
- Pest control services must occur at least monthly  
- Reports must be retained for a minimum of 12 months  
- Facilities must document internal monitoring findings

SECTION 8 — FACILITY MANAGEMENT RESPONSIBILITIES
8.1 Person-In-Charge (PIC) Duties  
- Ensure staff compliance  
- Maintain logs and documentation  
- Verify corrective actions  
- Oversee food safety training  

8.2 Staff Training  
Employees must be trained in:
- Personal hygiene  
- Safe food temperatures  
- Approved thawing methods  
- Cross-contamination prevention  
- Proper equipment sanitation  
- Chemical safety

SECTION 9 — EMERGENCY PROCEDURES
9.1 Power Outage  
- Discard foods held above 41°F for more than 2 hours  
- Document product losses  
- Notify health department if closures are required

9.2 Sewage Backup  
- Immediate closure required  
- Professional cleaning must occur  
- Inspector must verify corrections before reopening

9.3 Water Interruption  
- Facility must close until potable water is restored  
- Bottled water may be used for limited operations only with prior approval

CONCLUSION
These guidelines establish the minimum hygiene and food safety standards required in all food service establishments. Consistent adherence to these rules is necessary for preventing foodborne illness and ensuring public health.

END OF DOCUMENT

RESTAURANT INSPECTION REPORT – COUNTY PUBLIC HEALTH DEPARTMENT
Facility Name: Rangoli Sweets and Snacks
Address: 130 El Camino Real, San Jose, CA
Inspection Date: March 4, 2026
Inspection Type: Routine Compliance Inspection
Permit Number: RSN-440182

SECTION 1 — GENERAL OBSERVATIONS
Upon arrival, the inspector noted that the restaurant was open for regular business hours, with customers entering and exiting. The dining area maintained acceptable cleanliness standards. Floors were wiped recently, and tables appeared clean. Several employees were present, including cooks, cashiers, and an individual responsible for maintaining the display cases of sweets.

SECTION 2 — FOOD DISPLAY CONDITIONS
A significant portion of the inspection focused on the sweet display station. The display case contained confectioneries including jalebi, kaju katli, barfi, and assorted laddus. Several items displayed signs of dryness and discoloration, suggesting prolonged exposure to air. The inspector noted cracking on the surface of certain pieces of barfi and slight hardening on laddus. These conditions indicate that the items may have been left unrefrigerated for more than recommended durations.

Additionally, the upper display shelf was not fully enclosed. Two trays of sweets on the top shelf were exposed to ambient air without protective covering. Condensation was visible inside the glass case near the right-hand corner—an indicator of temperature imbalance. The combination of uncovered trays and condensation suggests inconsistent handling and possible microbial growth risk.

SECTION 3 — FOOD STORAGE AND TEMPERATURE CONTROL
A temperature scan of the refrigerated unit revealed fluctuating values between 45°F and 52°F. The acceptable holding temperature for ready-to-eat sweets is at or below 41°F to limit bacterial growth. Staff explained that the cooling unit “takes time to stabilize after opening,” but inspectors concluded that the equipment failed to meet minimum regulatory standards.

Inspection revealed boxes of raw ingredients stored near cleaning supplies, posing cross-contamination risk. A bag of flour was placed adjacent to detergent bottles. Baking trays with residue were stacked without thorough washing.

SECTION 4 — KITCHEN SANITATION FINDINGS
The kitchen area showed mixed compliance. Positives included:
- Dedicated handwashing sink with soap and paper towels
- Food-grade cutting boards labeled for specific uses
- Staff wearing hair coverings

Concerns noted:
- Excess oil buildup on fryers
- Improper wiping cloth storage (cloths left damp on counters)
- Unlabeled storage containers
- Dishes found drying next to open trash bins

SECTION 5 — EMPLOYEE PRACTICES
Two employees were observed handling ready‑to‑eat sweets with bare hands. When interviewed, they stated that “customers prefer fresh food touched by hand.” This violates county hygiene requirements. Gloves or utensils must be used.

One employee was observed touching a refrigerator handle and immediately resuming food handling without handwashing. The facility must reinforce hygiene training and proper handwashing frequency.

SECTION 6 — WASTE DISPOSAL AND VERMINT CONTROL
The restaurant’s waste disposal practices require improvement. There were minor signs of pest activity near the rear exit:
- Small black specks consistent with rodent droppings
- Visible beetle near the waste bin area
- Waste bags not sealed completely
- Drainpipe residue suggesting irregular cleaning

The grease trap outside the facility had mild overflow residue. This can attract pests if not managed.

SECTION 7 — SUMMARY OF VIOLATIONS AND REQUIRED ACTIONS
1. Temperature violations in food display cooler
2.

Improperly stored raw ingredients and cleaning chemicals
3. Use of bare hands for ready‑to‑eat sweets
4. Evidence of pest activity near waste disposal
5. Uncovered sweets in upper display case
6. Insufficient sanitation maintenance in kitchen equipment

Corrective actions required within 10 business days:
- Repair or replace cooling unit
- Implement covering protocols for display trays
- Provide hygiene retraining for all staff
- Deep clean waste disposal area
- Adjust kitchen cleaning schedule to include fryers and counters
- Verify pest control service within 2 weeks

RESTAURANT INSPECTION REPORT – COUNTY PUBLIC HEALTH DEPARTMENT
Facility Name: Moonlight Garden Restaurant & Banquet Hall
Address: 455 Blossom Terrace, Santa Clara, CA
Inspection Date: April 12, 2026
Inspection Type: Follow-Up Inspection (Post‑Violation Review)
Permit Number: MGR-552901

SECTION 1 — INITIAL CONDITIONS
The inspector arrived at approximately 9:10 AM. The restaurant was preparing for the lunch buffet service scheduled to begin at 11:00 AM. Staff were present in both the buffet line area and kitchen. Ambient temperature in the facility measured 71°F.

Since the previous inspection on March 27, Moonlight Garden was issued three corrective action notices:
1. Inconsistent dishwashing temperatures
2. Standing water in mop sink area
3. Improper thawing of raw chicken

SECTION 2 — BUFFET LINE REVIEW
The buffet warmers were operational but warming trays displayed uneven temperature distribution. The left-most warming unit had a measured temperature of 118°F, while the right-most read 132°F. Food safety regulations require hot-holding at or above 135°F.

The following items were placed in warmers prematurely:
- Paneer tikka (temperature: 112°F)
- Chana masala (temperature: 108°F)
- Vegetable biryani (temperature: 115°F)

A staff member explained that food was moved early "to get ahead of the rush." This practice increases bacterial growth risk and violates the county’s hot-holding rules.

SECTION 3 — FOOD PREPARATION AREA
The primary kitchen was significantly cleaner than previous visits, showing evidence of improved compliance. Observed improvements:
- Cutting boards were properly sanitized and stored vertically
- New utensil holders installed
- Mop sink area cleared and dried
- Dishwashing rinse temperatures consistently maintained at 182°F

Remaining concerns:
- A bowl of thawing chicken left at room temperature on a metal counter
- Raw chicken juice dripping near vegetable preparation station
- Employee cracked eggs and used the same unwashed hands to adjust the stove dial

SECTION 4 — HANDWASHING COMPLIANCE
Handwashing compliance had improved overall. Three staff members washed hands before switching tasks. However, one cook moved from handling poultry to chopping tomatoes without washing hands.

One staff member kept hand sanitizer next to the spice containers and used sanitizer instead of proper handwashing. Sanitizer alone is not sufficient; soap and water must be used for at least 20 seconds.

Handwashing station availability:
- Station #1 (north wall): Operational with soap and towels
- Station #2 (prep room): Operational, but towels were nearly depleted
- Station #3 (near dishwashing): Sink partially obstructed by stacked pans

SECTION 5 — SANITATION AND EQUIPMENT
The inspector noted several sanitation issues needing correction:
- Grease accumulation inside oven vents
- Excessive steaming condensation dripping from overhead exhaust line
- Several food containers unlabeled
- Rice cookers with hardened residue along inner surface

Dishwasher logs showed entries for calibration checks, but times were inconsistent. The inspector advised the manager to standardize logs.

SECTION 6 — PEST CONTROL AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
Waste bins outside the facility were found with partially open lids. Visible fruit flies hovered near one bin.

Staff stated the bins were “newly replaced” but did not demonstrate awareness about sealing requirements.

Pest control contractor report (submitted by management):
- Last visit: April 2
- Findings: No rodent activity; moderate fruit fly presence
- Corrective actions: Clean drains weekly, seal bin lids completely

Internal waste area inspection revealed:
- Wiping cloths stored on a cart near trash bin
- Excess moisture on floor due to inconsistent mopping
- Discarded vegetable scraps on prep counter near slow-moving drain

SECTION 7 — EMPLOYEE BEHAVIOR AND POLICY COMPLIANCE
Employees maintained generally positive compliance with attire rules. Hair coverings were worn by 90% of staff. One employee lacked a hair restraint and was asked to apply one.

The inspector reviewed the food safety training sign-off sheet. Eight employees completed training on April 5. Two employees (night shift) had not yet attended mandatory hygiene review.

Four employees spoke briefly with inspector and shared concerns about:
- Busy hours preventing adherence to handwashing frequency
- Difficulty maintaining food at proper warmer temperature during buffet service
- Inadequate communication between morning and lunch shift

SECTION 8 — SUMMARY OF VIOLATIONS
Violations observed during this follow-up inspection:
1. Premature placement of food in hot-holding warmers
2. Thawing raw poultry at room temperature
3. Cross-contamination risk with vegetable prep station
4. Insufficient towel supply at prep handwashing station
5. Improper use of sanitizer instead of handwashing
6. Fruit fly activity near outdoor waste bins
7. Temperature irregularities in buffet warmers

Management was instructed to:
- Use probe thermometers consistently
- Assign staff member to monitor warmer temperatures every 30 minutes
- Reinforce handwashing during shift transitions
- Install signage near buffet line regarding safe food temperatures

Facility is scheduled for another follow-up on May 3, 2026.

SECTION 1 — FACILITY OVERVIEW
Fox Chicken Sandwich & Grill is a mid-size dine‑in and takeout establishment specializing in grilled chicken sandwiches, fries, and salads. The restaurant operates daily from 10:00 AM to 9:00 PM. The inspection began at 2:37 PM during active lunchtime operations. Approximately 22 customers were present.

The dining area was generally tidy, with trash bins not overflowing. Tables were promptly wiped by staff after customer departure. Flooring near the drink dispenser contained minor sticky residue, likely from spilled soda.

SECTION 2 — FOOD HANDLING AND PREPARATION
The inspector observed food handling operations at the main sandwich station. Staff were preparing grilled chicken, slicing vegetables, and assembling sandwiches.

Key observations:
- Grill operator used separate utensils for raw and cooked chicken.
- Raw chicken stored at 36°F, which is compliant.
- Cooked chicken held at 140°F on the warming tray — compliant.
- However, tomatoes were stored in a metal container without ice, reading 52°F, exceeding the maximum allowable 41°F for cut vegetables.

A bag of mixed salad greens was opened but not sealed after partial use. Exposure to oxygen accelerates spoilage and microbial growth.

SECTION 3 — CROSS-CONTAMINATION RISKS
Cross-contamination risks were identified primarily near the assembly counter:
1. Cutting boards stacked while still wet, which can promote bacterial growth.
2. Employee placed raw chicken packaging on top of cooked chicken prep table.
3. Knife used for slicing onions was briefly placed into a container of cooked fries.
4.

Storage shelf above the grill contained cleaning chemicals and spray bottles.

Employees must maintain separation of raw and ready‑to‑eat foods at all times. Chemical storage must be relocated.

SECTION 4 — EQUIPMENT AND SANITATION
The inspector evaluated equipment sanitation:
- Sandwich grill: moderate grease accumulation around edges
- Deep fryers: acceptable condition but oil appeared slightly cloudy
- Refrigeration unit: working but gasket had torn edges
- Floor drains: residue buildup noted, requiring deep cleaning
- Microwave interior: splatter residue on upper panel

The manager stated that the fry oil was scheduled for replacement “later this afternoon.” Oil clarity indicated it may have been overdue.

Dishwashing station temperatures were mixed:
- Wash: 148°F (acceptable)
- Rinse: 167°F (acceptable)
- Sanitizer: 146°F (higher than recommended; sanitizer should not exceed 120°F)

Temperature logs were missing entries for three days.

SECTION 5 — HANDWASHING AND EMPLOYEE PRACTICES
Handwashing compliance was mostly satisfactory but not consistent:
- One staff member washed hands before changing tasks.
- Another employee handled cash, then resumed sandwich assembly without washing hands.
- Gloves were used but not replaced frequently enough.

A staff member was observed wiping sweat from forehead with gloved hand, then continuing food prep. Gloves must be replaced after contamination.

Hair restraints were worn by all employees except one line cook who had long hair uncovered. Manager corrected the issue immediately.

SECTION 6 — PEST CONTROL FINDINGS
Signs of potential pest activity were observed in storage and waste areas:
- Flour sacks showed minor gnaw marks.
- Two live ants spotted near the back storage shelf.
- Cardboard packaging left directly on floor.
- Grease buildup near outdoor dumpster area could attract pests.

The facility’s pest control log indicated:
- Last treatment: May 8
- Notes: “Monitor for ants near storage shelves.”

However, employee reports stated occasional “tiny insects near soda machine.”

SECTION 7 — WASTE AND WATER MANAGEMENT
Waste bin lids inside the kitchen were partially open. Food scraps were found around the bin edges. A mop bucket contained visibly dirty water and was stored next to food crates.

The soda machine drain tray contained mildew-like residue. Water lines needed flushing. Ice machine inspection revealed minimal buildup but required sanitizing due to seasonal increase in use.

SECTION 8 — STORAGE AND ORGANIZATION
Storage room observations included:
- Unlabeled spice containers
- Open bag of fries stored next to cleaning chemical spray
- Excess condensation inside cooling unit
- Unorganized shelves with improperly stacked items

Proper labeling and separation of chemicals from food items was stressed during the inspection.

SECTION 9 — SUMMARY OF VIOLATIONS
Violations during this inspection include:
1. Improper cold-holding temperature for tomatoes
2. Unsealed bags of salad greens
3. Raw chicken packaging placed near cooked food
4.

Chemicals stored above food prep areas
5. Grill grease accumulation
6. Missing temperature logs
7. Ant activity in storage area
8. Open waste bin lids and food debris
9. Improper glove use and inconsistent handwashing

Actions required within 7 business days:
- Repair or replace refrigerator gasket
- Relocate chemical storage
- Deep clean floor drains and grill area
- Flush soda machine drain line

RESTAURANT KITCHEN SANITATION MANUAL  
County Environmental Health Department  
2026 Edition  

INTRODUCTION  
This manual outlines the minimum sanitation standards required for all commercial restaurant kitchens. It provides detailed guidance on cleaning practices, equipment maintenance, contamination prevention, and operational hygiene. All food facilities are responsible for reviewing these standards regularly and ensuring adherence.

SECTION 1 — DAILY KITCHEN CLEANING TASKS  
1.1 Prep Surfaces  
All prep tables must be cleaned and sanitized every 4 hours during active food preparation. Approved sanitizers include quaternary ammonia and chlorine-based solutions. Surfaces must be wiped with single-use towels or designated sanitizing cloths stored in sanitizer buckets.

1.2 Cooking Equipment  
Grills, griddles, stovetops, fryers, and ovens must be wiped down at the end of the day. Grease buildup along grill edges and fryer walls should be removed before the next shift begins. Excess grease is a fire hazard and a magnet for pests.

1.3 Sinks and Faucets  
Handwashing and prep sinks must remain unobstructed. Sinks must be scrubbed daily with detergent, followed by sanitizing. Faucet handles must be disinfected, as they accumulate bacteria through repeated touch.

1.4 Refrigeration Units  
Shelves inside refrigeration units must be wiped daily. Any spills or leaks should be cleaned immediately. The gasket around the refrigerator door must be inspected regularly for cracks, mold, and residue.

SECTION 2 — WEEKLY KITCHEN CLEANING TASKS  
2.1 Exhaust Hoods  
Exhaust hoods accumulate grease from cooking vapors. Filters must be removed weekly and washed in hot, soapy water. Persistent residue must be removed using degreaser.

2.2 Storage Shelves  
Dry storage shelves should be wiped and sanitized weekly. Unlabeled containers must be discarded or properly labeled to avoid cross‑contamination.

2.3 Beverage Machines  
Coffee makers, soda dispensers, and juice machines must be flushed and cleaned weekly to prevent bacterial buildup. Drip trays and internal water lines should be cleaned using food-safe cleaners.

2.4 Trash and Waste Areas  
Indoor trash bins must be washed and sanitized weekly. Trash room floors and walls should be cleaned of food residue. Grease traps must be inspected weekly.

SECTION 3 — MONTHLY CLEANING TASKS  
3.1 Large Equipment  
Areas behind large appliances—grills, fryers, freezers, ovens—must be cleaned monthly or more frequently depending on grease accumulation. Dust, debris, and grease attract pests.

3.2 Ice Machines  
Ice machine interiors must be sanitized monthly to prevent mold. Ice trays must be deep cleaned using approved sanitizers.

3.3 Vents and Ceiling Panels  
Ceiling vents accumulate dust and airborne grease. These must be vacuumed and washed monthly.

SECTION 4 — SANITATION OF UTENSILS AND SMALLWARE  
4.1 Cutting Boards  
Cutting boards must be sanitized after each use. Deep grooves in boards indicate potential bacterial harborage and require replacement. A color-coding system is strongly recommended:
- Green: Produce  
- Red: Raw meat  
- Yellow: Poultry  
- Blue: Seafood  
- White: Ready-to-eat foods  

4.2 Knives and Tools  
Knives must be cleaned after each task. Leaving knives on cutting boards or sinks without washing contributes to contamination.

4.3 Storage Containers  
All containers must be food-grade, labeled, and stored with lids on. Containers with cracks must be discarded immediately.

SECTION 5 — EMPLOYEE SANITATION PRACTICES  
5.1 Hand Hygiene  
Employees must follow the county handwashing protocol:
- Use warm water and soap  
- Wash hands for 20 seconds  
- Dry using paper towels  
- Avoid touching hair, face, or clothing during prep  

5.2 Glove Usage  
Gloves must be replaced:
- After handling raw foods  
- After touching non-food items  
- After contamination (touching hair or trash)  
- Every 4 hours during continuous use  

5.3 Attire  
Hair restraints, clean aprons, closed-toe slip-resistant shoes, and minimal jewelry are required. Aprons must be replaced daily or when soiled.

SECTION 6 — CHEMICAL HANDLING AND STORAGE  
6.1 Chemical Safety  
Chemicals must be stored away from food-contact surfaces. Spray bottles must be clearly labeled. Cleaning chemicals must never be stored above food items.

6.2 Sanitizer Buckets  
Sanitizer buckets must contain solutions at proper concentration:
- Quaternary ammonia: 200–400 ppm  
- Chlorine: 50–100 ppm  

Test strips must be used to verify accurate strength.

SECTION 7 — WATER AND PLUMBING  
7.1 Water Temperature  
Hot water must reach at least 120°F at sinks used for dishwashing. Cold water must remain potable and free from contamination.

7.2 Drain Maintenance  
Floor drains must be scrubbed daily.

Drain covers must be removed weekly for deep cleaning. Drains showing residue or slow drainage require immediate attention.

SECTION 8 — SEWAGE AND EMERGENCY CLEANING  
8.1 Sewage Incidents  
Any sewage backup requires immediate closure of the facility.

Contaminated surfaces must undergo professional cleaning. Operations may resume only after reinspection.

8.2 Flooding Events  
Flooding from external sources requires removal of affected ingredients and thorough cleaning.

SECTION 9 — EVIDENCE OF NON‑COMPLIANCE  
Signs of insufficient sanitation include:
- Grease buildup  
- Mold growth  
- Unlabeled containers  
- Pest activity  
- Residue on cutting boards  
- Dirty ice machine components  
- Standing water  
- Sticky floors  

SECTION 10 — MANAGEMENT CHECKLIST  
Daily Checklist:
- Prep surfaces sanitized  
- Waste bins sealed  
- Gloves available  
- Handwashing supplies stocked  
- Refrigerator temperatures logged  
- Drain covers cleaned  

Weekly Checklist:
- Exhaust hood cleaned  
- Storage shelves sanitized  
- Trash room cleaned  
- Beverage machines flushed  

Monthly Checklist:
- Ice machines sanitized  
- Vents cleaned  
- Behind appliances cleaned  

CONCLUSION  
Maintaining a sanitized kitchen is vital for preventing foodborne illness. Managers must ensure daily, weekly, and monthly cleaning tasks are consistently followed, and corrective actions documented.
